This dashboard provides the detailed, step-by-step explanation and interactive match evidence.

Our approach combines context-rich, LLM-assisted cricket annotations with delivery-by-delivery match data to estimate pressure for each team before every ball.
We then assess how much each player helps reduce their team's pressure, and how reliably they do so across IPL and men's T20I matches.

01 / UNDERSTANDING PRESSURE

What is pressure in cricket?

A straightforward definition, with match examples instead of complicated charts.

In simple terms

  • Every team has an objective. The batting team must score enough runs or complete a chase. The bowling team must restrict those runs or defend a target.
  • Every objective depends on resources. The main resources are runs, balls remaining, wickets in hand, available batters, available bowlers and the match situation.
  • Pressure increases when the objective becomes harder with the resources left. Needing more runs with fewer balls or having fewer wickets available can increase batting pressure. A bowler facing a powerful, established batting partnership can experience bowling-side pressure.
  • Pressure is recalculated before every delivery. One dot, wicket, boundary or partnership can change the resources and the team's options for the next ball.
  • The same event has different effects in different situations. A dot ball when 10 are needed off 3 balls is far more costly than a dot when 80 are needed off 65.

Two examples that explain the idea

  • 100 runs from 15 balls versus 100 from 70 balls: The first chase has much higher pressure because the team has far less time to achieve the same objective, assuming other resources are comparable. Now introduce wickets lost, set batters and available bowling, and the full context becomes more precise.
  • Both teams are 84/4 after ten overs: Team A was 24/4 and rebuilt; Team B was 70/0 and just lost four wickets. The score is identical, but Team A may have two settled batters while Team B has new players at the crease. The delivery history helps explain their different current options.
The central idea: Pressure is not a label for a bad score. It is the difficulty of achieving the team's objective with the resources and context available at that instant.
02 / OUR APPROACH

How we turn every ball into a pressure reading

The method in seven clear steps, from the historical data to a player's final rating.

  1. Start with a historical backbone. Use IPL and men's T20 International delivery-level data from 2022 to 2024 to learn what normal and difficult match situations look like.
  2. Reconstruct the match before every ball. Record the score, target, wickets, legal balls left, batters at the crease, bowler and recent sequence of events. This gives the exact state in which a decision or action occurs.
  3. Add cricket context through 190 factors. Group the signals into 12 families, including chase equation, remaining batting and bowling resources, partnerships, recent dots and wickets, phase, venue, form, matchups and match stakes. The factor explorer below explains each family.
  4. Annotate pressure severity. The proposed 50 specialist LLM agent review streams examine contextual factors, suggest severity labels and highlight disagreements. Human I verify the important or disputed states and assign or confirm labels on a 0 to 5 scale.
  5. Learn how factors work together. Use the annotated historical situations to train and calibrate the pressure function. Factor importance depends on context: an opener's wicket matters differently in over 2 and over 17, and a dot ball matters differently in a comfortable chase and a tight finish.
  6. Produce a 0 to 10 reading for each team, on each delivery. Compute batting-team pressure and bowling-team pressure separately. They describe different objectives and are not required to add up to 10. Recompute both after each delivery to capture the changing situation.
  7. Measure player impact and consistency. Compare what the player actually achieved with a comparable expected response in the same situation. Calculate the extra pressure reduced by the player across deliveries and innings, then combine relief and reliability into the Pressure DNA Rating for the 2025 to 2026 IPL and T20I player window.
In one line: Match data → 190 contextual factors → agent and analyst annotations → learned pressure index → player relief versus expectation → reliability-adjusted ranking.

The factor explorer, rating method and real innings below provide the detail behind each step. Data availability differs by factor, so external conditions and matchup inputs require their own verification.

04 / PRESSURE ANNOTATION AND MODEL

How does a match state become a pressure index?

From historical research and ball-level annotation to a learned index and player evaluation.

Our research and modelling approach

We start with real match history, reconstruct the situation before each delivery, and connect cricket context with analyst-reviewed pressure severity. The sequence below explains the complete approach before the formulas.

  • Build the historical backbone (2022 to 2024). We collected IPL and men's T20I delivery-level records and calculated historical reference patterns for scoring, wickets, roles and innings phases. These give the system its cricketing baseline.
  • Reconstruct the context before every delivery. We rebuild the score, target, legal balls remaining, wickets, partnership, batters, bowler and recent sequence of runs, dots and dismissals. Only information available before that delivery enters its pre-ball prediction.
  • Define 190 contextual feature slots across 12 families. They describe the available resources and the difficulty of achieving the objective: chase equation, batting and bowling resources, partnerships, momentum, venue, player roles, form, matchup, team strength, match stakes and conditions. Feature availability is verified against its source.
  • Specify the LLM-assisted annotation process. The proposed workflow uses 50 specialized LLM-agent review streams to assess historical states and propose a pressure-severity label from 0 to 5 separately for each team's objective. Each reviewer considers the combined cricket context, not just a single ball outcome.
  • Add human analyst verification. I review the agent rationales, compare disagreements, check unusual situations and confirm the final training labels. The annotations are the most important supervision signal because they teach the model how difficult each state actually is.
  • Learn the factor relationships and interactions. With verified labels, the training stage fits a severity model from historical input vectors. Its learned weights can depend on context. A dot ball in a comfortable powerplay is not assigned the same effect as a dot ball in a last-over chase; an opener's wicket early in the innings is different from one late in the innings.
  • Calibrate two pressure indices from 0 to 10. The model converts the predicted 0–5 severity to a calibrated batting-team pressure reading and a separate bowling-team pressure reading. Both update as the resource situation changes, and they do not have to sum to ten.
  • Apply the model to the 2025 and 2026 IPL and men's T20I seasons. Once trained and validated on historical data, the same pre-delivery calculation runs throughout each newer innings. We compare each player's actual response against a role-and-context expectation to estimate additional pressure relief, then combine that with consistency across pressure opportunities for the final player rating.
Two numbers to understand: a factor describes the match situation, while an annotation captures how difficult the team's objective is in that combined situation. The model learns the relationship, then the charts below explain the mathematics and cricket examples.
A / ANNOTATION SCALE

What does a 0–5 label mean?

0–1Comfortable. The objective is achievable with generous resources.
2Manageable. Some constraints, but reasonable recovery options.
3Meaningful pressure. Wickets, time or scoring options are becoming scarce.
4Severe pressure. Recovery needs a significantly better-than-ordinary response.
5Extreme. The objective is very difficult given the available resources.

Labels are assessed separately for the batting and bowling teams. They describe difficulty, not an individual player's ability.

B / MODEL LEARNING

How do the factors get their weight?

Each annotated ball has an input vector x containing its contextual factors and a verified severity label y. The model learns the relationship by minimizing prediction error across historical situations.

xt = [x1, x2, …, x190]
ŝt = fθ(xt) (severity 0–5)
Pt = 10 · C(ŝt / 5) (index 0–10)

Here fθ is the learned severity function and C is a calibration mapping. Factor weights are learned together and can interact. A dot ball's effect depends on phase and remaining runs; there is no fixed “dot-ball penalty”.

Two separate predictions: Pbatting for the scoring team's objective and Pbowling for the defending team's objective. They are not complements and need not add to 10.

D / ONE STATE, THREE POSSIBLE DELIVERIES

Why a dot, six and wicket affect pressure differently

Suppose a team needs 24 runs from 12 balls with four wickets remaining. The index before the ball is 7.4/10. Each row is a separate possible outcome from that same state.

DOT BALL
7.4 → 8.1

One ball disappears with no run. Pressure rises by 0.7.

SIX
7.4 → 5.8

The equation improves to 18 from 11. Pressure falls by 1.6.

WICKET
7.4 → 8.7

Another batting resource is lost. Pressure rises by 1.3.

Team relief on a ball = pressure before − pressure after

The branch indices are worked examples used to explain the direction and magnitude of a state change. Player attribution requires a separate expected-response comparison, described in the next section.

What is stored for every delivery?

The pre-ball match state, contextual factors, annotations and analyst review, separate batting/bowling pressure readings, the observed outcome, the next-ball state and the explanation of which resource changes mattered. This is the intended inference procedure for IPL and men's T20I innings. Current match events and historical reference patterns are real; the full 50-agent annotation run and trained 190-factor pressure model have not been independently validated in this dashboard.

05 / FROM PRESSURE TO PLAYER IMPACT

How do we know who actually helped?

A six-step explanation of pressure relief, without confusing the team's improvement with an individual player's credit.

  1. Identify when pressure exists. Before every delivery, read the batting and bowling teams' separate 0 to 10 pressure indices. A player can inherit a difficult situation or encounter it later in the innings.
  2. Record the situation before the ball. Capture the objective, runs, balls, wickets, active batters and bowlers, match phase, recent events and relevant historical context. This freezes the starting point for a fair comparison.
  3. Measure what the player actually did. For a batter, track the runs, dots, boundaries, strike rotation and the effect on the chase or scoring equation. For a bowler, track conceded runs, wickets and how the opponent's scoring options change.
  4. Compare with an expected player in the same situation. Use the historical role-and-phase reference and, when verified, venue and matchup inputs. Calculate what the pressure would look like after a typical response.
  5. Attribute the extra pressure relief. Subtract the actual post-ball pressure from the expected post-ball pressure. Credit a player for their own response rather than for a partner's boundary or another player's wicket. A worse-than-expected response receives negative credit.
  6. Repeat across balls and pressure innings. Sum the delivery contributions, normalize by pressure faced, and assess whether positive relief is repeated across 2025 and 2026 IPL and men's T20I games. Combine relief percentage with a sample-size-aware consistency score to obtain the Pressure DNA Rating.
Pressure relief on one delivery: expected pressure after a comparable response − actual team pressure after this player's response. Positive means the player did more to restore control than expected.
A concrete exampleTilak hits a six in a difficult chase.

Instead of judging the six only as six runs, compare the new chase equation with the pressure after a typical middle-order delivery in that exact situation. The difference is the estimated extra contribution of Tilak's ball. If the non-striker later gets out, Tilak does not receive credit or blame for that delivery.

The final ranking combinesRelief % × Reliability % ÷ 100

The same logic applies to bowlers, using bowling-team pressure. A low-cost, wicket-taking spell can reduce pressure even if the batting side later wins.

09 / FEATURED BOWLER

Krunal Pandya. Six balls of control.

IPL · 22 March 2025
How to read Krunal's pressure over
  • Situation: KKR were 107/2 after ten overs. Krunal's over is evaluated from the defending team's perspective.
  • Six selectable balls: Each chip gives the actual result and the bowling-team pressure reading before and after that ball.
  • Positive team relief: A lower bowling pressure means the fielding side has regained control. Wickets and dot balls can matter more than merely conceding few runs.
  • Player credit versus team change: The change from 7.40 to 4.70 is a team-state movement. Isolating Krunal's above-expected impact requires comparing his outcomes with a comparable bowler in that context.

THE PRESSURE DNA THESIS

A better question leads to a better ranking.

Not simply “who scored the most?” or “who took the most wickets?” but who made the biggest, most repeatable improvement to the team's resource position when the objective was genuinely difficult?

The present per-delivery 0–10 readings use analyst-assigned checkpoints and context rules; player-wide relief percentages are scenario-calibrated to demonstrate the ranking method.
